newsitem.title: USA: Gore to raise funding issues with Chinese.
newsitem.headline: Gore to raise funding issues with Chinese.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore on Saturday began an eight-day trip to Asia aimed at easing strains in U.S.-Sino relations, saying he intended to discuss allegations China illegally tried to influence the 1996 U.S. elections.
Gore told reporters onboard Air Force Two that he intended to raise the issue in Beijing "in an appropriate way and in the proper context" but stressed that "this is not what this trip is about."

Stressing that China vigorously denied charges being investigated by the FBI that it tried to funnel money into presidential and some congressional campaigns, Gore said he would discuss the matter "in an appropriate and sensitive way."

After stopping in Alaska to refuel his plane, Gore headed to Japan, where he planned to discuss China policies and other issues with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday before heading to Beijing that night.
Gore's talks on Tuesday with Chinese President Jiang Zemin, the first prolonged U.S. discussions with Beijing's leader since the death of Deng Xiaoping, who died last month.

"I think its a more propicious time now than in the past because both our countries are clearly signaling to one another that we want to find a way to move forward in the relationship" between Washington and Beijing, Gore said.
U.S. officials were closely monitoring the situation in China for any hint that Jiang's power may be threatened now that Deng, his political patron, has passed away.
Gore quietly will be taking the measure of Jiang himself and his ability to fend off any would-be rivals, officials said.

A broad range of divisive issues, from trade to human rights, faced the mission by Gore -- the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit Beijing since Army troops brutally ended pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in 1989.

Gore defended President Bill Clinton's decision to drop his initial demands that China show progress on human rights in order to renew most favored nation trade status, which eases tariffs on goods sold in the United States.
"It is more than reasonable to place a bet that as the free market expands dramatically, so too will democracy," said Gore, who noted that "change is taking place rapidly" in China.

A primary purpose of the trip was to lay the groundwork for a state visit to Washington by Jiang later this year and a trip to Bejing by Clinton in 1998. Gore said he did not expect exact dates to be agreed to because they were "still a long way off."

Concerns about the fund-raising scandal involving China dampened some of the expectations for the trip. Although U.S. officials were negotiating with their Chinese counterparts trying to hammer out various agreements in time for Gore's trip, no dramatic breakthroughs were expected.

In fact, Gore's advisers had a debate over whether he should even participate in a signing ceremony in which China plans to order new jet airplanes from Boeing Co., a move that will generate jobs and benefit the U.S. economy.
Although officials said there was no doubt Gore would participate in such an event if a final contract was reached, the fact there was any question underscored the sensitivity of the trip.

"My guess is, not much will be achieved here, and that's okay," said Greg Mastel, an expert on China for the Economic Strategy Institute, about the visit. "It's important to have an important dialogue with the Chinese."
"The problems we have with the Chinese are not the kind of problems you can solve with a simple summit ... but just keeping the dialogue open is useful," he said.
